clue.text: Bone-breakers aboard ship check quartzite?

indicators.note: to be aboard a vessel is to be inside it, so the following pieces go within the ship's letters

parts.note: SS is the abbreviation for steamship
to tick is to check off an item on a list
quartzite is sandstone transformed by heat and pressure, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: Something on board a ship is being inspected for a hard rock.
explanation.walkthrough: Quartzite is metamorphosed sandstone, so the question mark admits a definition by example; 'aboard ship' puts both pieces between the ship's two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery rhyme says sticks and stones may break my bones, so these are the proverbial bone-breakers.

clue.text: Maybe bad press is sadly what initiates recrimination and signals fracas

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters of the fodder are jumbled
what initiates a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of recrimination
a fracas is a noisy quarrel; rows are quarrels

explanation.surface: Negative coverage reads as accusations and warning signs of a brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' marks bad press as one example of the phrase, which comes from Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's 'slings and arrows of outrageous fortune' has become an idiom for hostile attacks, such as harsh criticism in newspapers.

clue.text: Help lifting hotel cases assigned to a Dr Jones

indicators.note: the hotel word encases, or holds inside it, the next piece

parts.note: an inn is a hotel

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting turns the word upward so it reads backwards

parts.note: aid means help

explanation.surface: A porter carries an archaeologist's luggage up through a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'lifting' turns the help word upwards; Dr Jones is the film hero's academic title.
explanation.definitionFit: Indiana Jones is the film archaeologist who holds a doctorate, so the doctor's first name is the answer.

clue.text: See 11
Certain users getting woozy inside trailer

indicators.note: inside places the jumbled letters within the advertisement word

parts.note: a trailer is a short advert for a film, so AD

indicators.note: woozy means unsteady and muddled, so the letters of users get mixed up

explanation.surface: People in a caravan feel lightheaded, though they are sure of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Assured is a synonym of certain, meaning confident or guaranteed beyond doubt.

clue.text: Shape with mould intricately set with acid

indicators.note: intricately suggests complex rearrangement, so the letters of set and acid are combined in a new order

explanation.surface: A craftsman forms something in a mould and finishes it with acid etching.
explanation.definitionFit: To die-cast is to make metal objects by forcing molten metal into a mould, a manufacturing process.

clue.text: Podium options for London tripper?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in zoology a podium is a ..., the small tubular limb of a starfish or sea urchin
second meaning: a visitor to London can get about by ... or on ...

explanation.walkthrough: The Tube is the London Underground. 'Podium' looks like a platform for winners, but it is the biologist's word for a starfish's tiny limb.
explanation.definitionFit: Echinoderms move on hydraulic tube feet, which zoologists call podia, while tourists travel by Underground or walking.

clue.text: Like strong men from the south, Type Ones forsake county

indicators.note: the letter I looks like the numeral one, and forsake means leave, so every I goes
in a down clue, reading from the south means reading upwards, so the phrase is reversed

parts.note: strong men are men of iron, so 'of iron' describes them
ilk means type or kind

explanation.surface: Muscle-bound visitors from down south, Type One personalities, abandon a rural region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From the south' turns OF IRON into NORIFO; ILK follows, and 'Ones forsake' drops both I letters from NORIFOILK.
explanation.definitionFit: Norfolk is an English county in East Anglia, on the coast north-east of London.

clue.text: Bozo, three sheets to wind, blathers

indicators.note: to wind something is to twist it about, so the letters are turned into a new order

explanation.surface: A drunken clown, three sheets to the wind, talks nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Three sheets to the wind' is an idiom for very drunk, which hides that 'to wind' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To shoot the breeze is an informal idiom for chatting idly, which is what someone who blathers does.

clue.text: Helpful figures retained by blind ice-skaters

indicators.note: retained by means held within, so the answer sits inside the letters of these words

explanation.surface: Sightless skaters keep hold of useful numbers to guide them.
explanation.definitionFit: Indices are numerical indicators, such as price indices, that help measure and compare things.

clue.text: Wallflower's plea to reverse ban?

indicators.note: to reverse something is to run it backwards, so the plea's letters are read from the end

parts.note: a wallflower, a shy person left out at a dance, might cry 'O grab me!'

explanation.surface: A shy dancer begs for someone to overturn a prohibition.
explanation.walkthrough: A wallflower is someone sitting out at a dance. Read backwards, 'O grab me' gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An embargo is an official ban, especially on trade with a particular country.

clue.text: Attempt to score set off "smart" guy, seizing crown from Kyrgios

parts.note: to go is to set off

indicators.note: seizing means grabbing hold of, so the guy's name takes the letter inside it

parts.note: a smart alick, a variant spelling of smart alec, so the guy is ALICK

indicators.note: the crown of a word is its top, its first letter

parts.note: first letter of Kyrgios

explanation.surface: A cocky man grabs the tennis player Nick Kyrgios's crown as he tries to win.
explanation.walkthrough: Smart alick is an accepted spelling of smart alec; K goes inside ALICK to give ALKICK.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a goal kick restarts play from the goal area, and any kick at goal is a scoring attempt.

clue.text: Item Elgar's kith and kin wanted for a new Variation? His idea too

indicators.note: a new variation on a theme rearranges it, so the letters of the fodder are reordered

explanation.surface: Elgar wonders whether his friends would want to feature in a new Enigma Variation.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter Elgar shares a name with the composer, whose Enigma Variations portrayed his friends. 'Wanted' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says clever people have the same thoughts, so it fits a person saying 'that was my idea too'.

clue.text: See 6
See 12
See 12
Ill at ease, an arty type joins cast

parts.note: an is the indefinite article, A
a BA is a Bachelor of Arts, an arts graduate
to cast skin or antlers is to shed them

explanation.surface: An artistic person, uncomfortable, joins a theatre company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like a group of actors, but it is a verb meaning throw off.
explanation.definitionFit: Abashed means embarrassed and self-conscious, which is a state of feeling uncomfortable.

clue.text: Offensive peasant's cutting wood

indicators.note: cutting into means going inside, so the peasant goes within the offensive

parts.note: the Tet Offensive was a major attack in the Vietnam War, named after the lunar new year festival
a hick is an unsophisticated country person; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: An unpleasant farm labourer is chopping timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offensive' looks like an adjective meaning rude; here it is the noun, the Tet Offensive of 1968.
explanation.definitionFit: A thicket is a dense growth of shrubs and small trees, a small area of woodland.

clue.text: Was stooping lower intended to miss end of eaves?

indicators.note: to miss means to lack, so the letter is left out

parts.note: designed means intended, as in designed to impress

indicators.note: end of a word is its last letter

parts.note: last letter of eaves

explanation.surface: A builder bending under the roof meant to avoid the edge of the eaves.
explanation.definitionFit: To deign is to condescend to do something, so someone who deigned was stooping beneath their dignity.

clue.text: A broadcaster opens financial note that is contemptible

indicators.note: the pieces open up the note by going into its middle

parts.note: an IOU is a written note acknowledging a debt
Sky is a British satellite broadcaster

explanation.surface: A television company starts up a money memo that is despicable.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation 'I ask you!' expresses scorn or disbelief at something shameful or ridiculous.

clue.text: Bottom of class, repeatedly last in school set, awkwardly wearing dunce's cap for all to see

indicators.note: wearing a dunce's cap means having its top letter put on as a hat, at the head of this down entry
the cap of a down word is its top letter, its first

parts.note: first letter of dunce
U is the film classification for universal viewing, suitable for all

indicators.note: last in means the final letter of the word

parts.note: last letter of school
repeatedly means the same letter is taken again

indicators.note: awkwardly means clumsily, so the letters of set are rearranged

explanation.surface: A poor pupil, always bottom, is made to wear the dunce's hat in public.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads bottom to top: the L pair and EST (from 'awkwardly' set) are wearing D and U above them, as a hat sits on a head in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The dullest pupil is the least intelligent, and so ranks lowest in the class.

clue.text: Little European pond-dweller

parts.note: a tad is a little bit
a Pole is a European from Poland

explanation.surface: A small creature from Europe lives in a pond.
explanation.definitionFit: A tadpole is the larval form of a frog or toad, which lives in ponds before maturing.

clue.text: See missing blended black tea exposed to other tea leaves?

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so the named letter is left out of the fodder
blended means mixed, so the remaining letters are jumbled

parts.note: see sounds like the letter C

explanation.surface: A tea-taster notes that a blend of black tea has come into contact with other varieties.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney rhyming slang a tea leaf is a thief, so something exposed to thieves can be taken. 'Other' separates these tea leaves from the black tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Something takable can be stolen, which is what being within reach of thieves implies.

clue.text: Like bottom feeders caught in a green uprising

indicators.note: in a down clue, an uprising reads from bottom to top, so the letters go backwards

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
eco- means environmentally friendly, or green

explanation.surface: Fish that feed on the seabed are trapped in a revolt by environmentalists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uprising' looks like a rebellion, but in a down clue it reverses the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Bottom feeders such as flatfish live on the floor of the sea, so they are creatures of the ocean.

clue.text: Name good time to avoid runs through to work

definitions.text: Name good time to avoid runs through to work

indicators.note: to avoid means to keep away, so the named letters are left out of the fodder
to work something is to knead it, so the remaining letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A commuter names the best moment to skip on a dash to the office.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines: the period when a commuter runs through crowds to work is one to avoid if you can.
explanation.definitionFit: The rush hour is the peak commuting period when roads and trains are crowded with people travelling to work.

clue.text: See 12
See 27
See 23
Resident in National Park, Four Seasons welcoming turn from Orbison

indicators.note: welcoming means taking in a guest, so the reversed nickname goes inside

parts.note: a year is made up of four seasons

indicators.note: turn means to turn around, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: Roy Orbison, the singer, was nicknamed the Big O

explanation.surface: A luxury hotel in a national park greets a performance by the singer Roy Orbison.
explanation.walkthrough: Four Seasons looks like the hotel chain, but it is a year.
explanation.definitionFit: Yogi Bear is the cartoon bear who lives in Jellystone Park, a parody of Yellowstone National Park.

clue.text: Protégé perhaps primarily obsessed by a post yet unfilled

indicators.note: post means after, so this piece is placed after the previous ones
primarily means firstly, so take the first letter

parts.note: first letter of obsessed
X means by, as in measurements such as three by four

indicators.note: unfilled means with the inside emptied, so only the outer letters remain

parts.note: the first and last letters of yet
a means one

explanation.surface: A mentor's favourite is fixated on a job that is still vacant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Protégé' looks like a person, but it is an example of a word stressed on its last syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: An oxytone is a word with the stress on its final syllable, as in the French pronunciation of protégé.

clue.text: Help one might have slicing cheese and chocolate cake

indicators.note: slicing means cutting into, so OWN goes into the cheese

parts.note: brie is a soft French cheese
to own something is to have it

explanation.surface: A sweet snack someone might eat along with sliced cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: A brownie is a helpful household sprite in folklore, so 'Help' is one definition and 'chocolate cake' another.
explanation.definitionFit: A brownie is a dense chocolate square, and in Scottish folklore a sprite that does housework at night.

clue.text: It's impossible to do Conservative parked on single yellow line

indicators.note: in an across clue, parked on means placed right next to, so the line follows

parts.note: a square is a conventional, old-fashioned person
the Circle line is the yellow line on the London Underground map, the only one in that colour

explanation.surface: A Tory leaves his car on a single yellow line, a parking restriction.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a single yellow line at the kerb restricts parking; here it is the Circle line, coloured yellow on the Tube map.
explanation.definitionFit: Squaring the circle, making a square of equal area to a circle, was proved impossible, so the idiom means attempting the impossible.
